newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia says undecided on S.African helicopters.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia says undecided on S.African helicopters.

text.p: Malaysia's Defence Minister Syed Hamid Albar said on Monday his government was interested in South Africa's Rooivalk combat helicopters, but had yet to decide on the purchase.

Armaments Corp of South Africa, maker of the Rooivalk, had been courting the Malaysian government for more than two years and renewed its campaign last week with the visit of President Nelson Mandela to Kuala Lumpur, defence sources said.
But Syed Hamid said the Malaysian government had yet to decide on the purchase.
"We've tested it...it's an attack helicopter and we're interested, but we've not come to a final decision," he told reporters in Kuala Lumpur after talks with French Defence Minister Charles Millon.
South African radio qouted government sources as saying Mandela sealed a deal with Malaysia for the first overseas sale of the Rooivalk during his five-day visit to Kuala Lumpur that ended on Monday.
Rooivalk manufacturer Denel said, however, it knew nothing of the deal.
Mandela's spokesman Parks Mankahlana said he was also in the dark about any agreement, but said more might become known when the president arrived back in the country at 1500 GMT.
Syed Hamid said U.S., British, Russian and French helicopter manufacturers were also offering machines to Malaysia and his government would base its decision on price and technology.

"The helicopter may be the best in the world but it still has to suit our needs," Syed Hamid said. "Suffice to say, the Rooivalk has the capability to fulfill at least part of our air force requirement."
He said if the purchase went through, the deal would include a local components manufacturing facility for the Rooivalk.

Malaysia has been building up its military capability in recent years, buying F-18 jets from the United States, MiG-29 fighters from Russia and armoured personnel carriers from South Korea while denying it was involved in an arms race.
The government's biggest defence project is a 15-year programme to acquire 27 naval patrol boats at a cost of 5.0 billion ringgit ($2 billion).
